children: By Michelle Hackman and Alexander Ward
A House hearing about worldwide threats turned into a broad discussion about a string of nationwide outages and disturbing intelligence about Iranian threats to the homeland.

Top Trump administration national-security officials testified on Capitol Hill on Wednesday, providing them with an opportunity to address what was behind a ground stop of flights and several service disruptions that affected millions of Americans.
The administration has come under intense criticism in recent days, including from former administration officials, for its inability to clearly explain what's behind the outages.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton appeared before the House Homeland Security Committee, along with FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia. Clayton, who was added to the hearing a day before the session, stated repeatedly that there was no coordinated attack on the U.S.
"We have no indication that these events are related," he said.

Mullin also addressed his trip to a college football game on a private plane — shortly after a nationwide ground stop of flights — saying it was a normal family trip and that canceling it would have raised concerns.
Clayton says string of outages aren't an attack
Clayton addressed a number of digital and network outages across the country, telling lawmakers that they are the result of technical updates and not an assault on the U.S.

"I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions," he said, but the service disruptions were "associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."
"We have no indication that these events are related," he said, adding that the U.S. intelligence community continues to investigate these and other issues.

Connecticut Rep. Jim Himes, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, released a statement echoing the administration's explanations. "I have seen no evidence to suggest any of the outages were the result of a malicious actor," he said. He said the "breakneck pace of patching" of outdated systems "could cause more frequent outages" but was necessary to get ahead of new cyber and AI-related threats.

In recent days, the Trump administration ordered a ground stop on all flights in the U.S., a classified intelligence network temporarily went down and Microsoft 365 products stopped working, among other problems. It led to speculation that perhaps they were all the result of a nefarious actor targeting the U.S.

Clayton was added to the hearing at the last minute to address the nation's growing concerns. Some of President Trump's political allies were frustrated by the administration's slow public-relations response.
Mullin says he flew to college football game to show trust in the system
Mullin has faced criticism over his decision to fly a government plane to the LSU-Texas college football game on Saturday, less than a day after the nationwide ground stop was lifted.

Mullin used his opening statement at the hearing to defend the trip, saying he went ahead because not doing so would look suspicious. He said the plan, to take his niece to the game, had been set for weeks.

"We had deep conversations about it," Mullin said. "And it came in that if we canceled something when the airspace would be completely open...it would show distrust that we aren't even willing to fly."
Mullin called members of Congress inquiring about the trip hypocritical.
"You would have done the same thing, except you would have called it a campaign event," he said.
'Heightened' threat from Iran to Americans, Clayton says
Clayton said that the U.S. faced a "heightened threat from the Iranian lethal plotting against our citizens at home and abroad."
"These threats have substantially increased," he said. "Our women and men abroad, our women and men here in the United States, are under greater threat."

Clayton was asked repeatedly about a CNN story on the U.S. collecting intelligence about an Iranian plot to detonate a "dirty bomb" in Washington. Clayton declined to address the intelligence directly, but used the indictment of an imprisoned man in New York accused of orchestrating plots against U.S. citizens and an attack on U.S. aircraft and pilots at a British military base as evidence of the danger Iran poses.
"That demonstrates a network capability that is very sophisticated, global, and one that we need to combat seriously with all the tools we have available," he said.
Mullin says he wasn't aware of Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

Rep. Seth Magaziner (D., R.I.) asked Mullin when he learned about the affair that Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia CEO last week, had with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have been working with Chinese intelligence, in light of reporting for months that other top administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, were aware of the affair.
"We weren't privileged to that information at all until it broke," Mullin replied.

Mullin has been on thin ice with White House officials for months following repeated verbal blunders, including remarks breaking with the administration on immigration enforcement and his suggestion, during Trump's Fourth of July celebration on the national mall, to cancel a fireworks display due to dangerous extreme heat that day.
"You're the homeland security secretary, you oversee the nation's premier cybersecurity agency. Why weren't you privy to this information?" Magaziner asked.
"If it were a direct threat to the homeland, I would have been read in on it," Mullin replied.
FBI official won't name a right-wing group that should be classified as a terrorist organization

Though it wasn't the primary subject of the hearing, Rep. Bennie Thompson (D., Miss.), the top Democrat on the committee, questioned the FBI's deputy director about a different administration initiative: to reclassify some left-wing groups as terrorist organizations.
When Thompson asked for examples of organizations that should be reclassified, Raia offered two: "I would say 764. I would also say antifa."
Thompson followed up, "So help me out, would any right-wing organizations meet that test?"
Raia repeatedly declined to name any, saying, "I don't want to paint a broad brush."
"There are people inside of right-wing organizations just like there are people inside of left-wing organizations," Raia said.
